L1139: `write_stdin` is transport for an existing unified-exec session. It doesn't run `PreToolUse` again when it sends input or polls a command that already passed `PreToolUse`.
L1140: 
L1141: Some specialized tool paths can opt out of the default hook path. Treat tool hooks as a useful guardrail, not a complete enforcement boundary.
L1142: ## Common input fields
L1143: 
L1144: Every command hook receives one JSON object on `stdin`.
L1145: 
L1146: These are the shared fields you will usually use:
L1147: Field  | Type  | Meaning
L1148: --- | --- | ---
L1149: `session_id`  | `string`  | Current Codex session id. Subagent hooks use the parent session id.
L1150: `transcript_path`  | `string | null`  | Path to the session transcript file, if any
L1151: `cwd`  | `string`  | Working directory for the session
L1152: `hook_event_name`  | `string`  | Current hook event name
L1153: `model`  | `string`  | Codex-specific extension. Active model slug
L1154: 
L1155: Turn-scoped hooks list `turn_id` as a Codex-specific extension in their event-specific tables.
L1156: `SessionStart`, `PreToolUse`, `PermissionRequest`, `PostToolUse`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `SubagentStart`, `SubagentStop`, `Stop`, and `Interrupt` also include `permission_mode`, which describes the current permission mode as `default`, `acceptEdits`, `plan`, `dontAsk`, or `bypassPermissions`.
L1157: 
L1158: `transcript_path` points to a chat transcript for convenience, but the transcript format isn't a stable interface for hooks and may change over time.
L1159: 
L1160: If you need the full wire format, see cite445†Schemas .
L1161: ## Common output fields
L1162: 
L1163: `SessionStart`, `PreCompact`, `PostCompact`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `SubagentStop`, and `Stop` support these shared JSON fields. `SubagentStart` accepts the same shape for `systemMessage` and hook-specific context, but `continue: false` doesn't stop the subagent:
L1164: 
L1165:     `{
L1166:       "continue": true,
L1167:       "stopReason": "optional",
L1168:       "systemMessage": "optional",
L1169:       "suppressOutput": false
L1170:     }`
L1171: Field  | Effect
L1172: --- | ---
L1173: `continue`  | If `false`, marks that hook run as stopped
L1174: `stopReason`  | Recorded as the reason for stopping
L1175: `systemMessage`  | Surfaced as a warning in the UI or event stream
L1176: `suppressOutput`  | Parsed today but not yet implemented
L1177: 
L1178: Exit `0` with no output is treated as success and Codex continues.
L1179: `PreToolUse` and `PermissionRequest` support `systemMessage`, but `continue`, `stopReason`, and `suppressOutput` aren't currently supported for those events. If a `PreToolUse` hook returns one of those unsupported fields, Codex marks that hook run as failed, reports the error, and continues the tool call.
L1180: 
L1181: `PostToolUse` supports `systemMessage`, `continue: false`, and `stopReason`. `suppressOutput` is parsed but not currently supported for that event.
L1182: ### Large hook output
L1183: 
L1184: By default, Codex limits each model-visible hook-output message to roughly 2,500 tokens. If a hook returns more, Codex saves the full text under `<temp_dir>/hook_outputs/<session_id>/<uuid>.txt` and gives the model a head-and-tail preview with the saved-file path. This behavior is called spilling: Codex stores oversized output on disk and replaces it with a shorter, model-visible preview. If the file can't be written, the model still receives a truncated preview.
L1185: Keep hook and plugin context concise. Context from multiple hooks and plugins adds up and can degrade model performance. Raising `additionalContextLimit` increases that risk. Avoid setting the limit to `0` unless the hook enforces a strict output cap; otherwise, a single hook can consume the entire context window.
L1186: For any command hook that returns `additionalContext`, set `additionalContextLimit` on the handler to customize the approximate token threshold:
L1187: 
L1188:     `{
L1189:       "type": "command",
L1190:       "command": "python3 ~/.codex/hooks/session_start.py",
L1191:       "additionalContextLimit": 5000
L1192:     }`
L1193: Omit `additionalContextLimit` to use the default `2500`-token threshold. Use a positive integer to select a different threshold, or `0` to pass the handler's complete additional context directly to the model. Codex evaluates each matching handler independently. For events that can't produce additional context, Codex ignores `additionalContextLimit` and reports a configuration warning.
L1194: 
L1195: The setting applies only to `additionalContext`. Tool feedback and continuation prompts keep the default limit.
L1196: Because oversized output can be written to disk, avoid returning secrets or other sensitive data in hook output.
L1197: ## Run hooks in the background
L1198: 
L1199: By default, Codex waits for a command hook to finish before continuing the operation that triggered it. Set `async` to `true` to run a command hook in the background while Codex continues.
L1271: ### SessionEnd
L1272: 
L1274: Switching away from a conversation or calling `thread/unsubscribe` doesn't end the session right away, so it won't immediately run `SessionEnd`. Your hook can still read the session transcript while it runs.
L1275: 
L1276: `matcher` filters `reason` for this event. For now, `reason` is always `other`. You can omit `matcher` or use `other` to run on every `SessionEnd` event.
L1277: 
L1278: Fields in addition to cite446†Common input fields :
L1279: 
L1280: Field  | Type  | Meaning
L1281: --- | --- | ---
L1282: `reason`  | `string`  | Why the session ended: `other`
L1283: For example, a `SessionEnd` command receives:
L1284: 
L1285:     `{
L1286:       "session_id": "thr_123",
L1287:       "transcript_path": "/workspace/.codex/rollout.jsonl",
L1288:       "cwd": "/workspace",
L1289:       "hook_event_name": "SessionEnd",
L1290:       "reason": "other"
L1291:     }`
L1292: 
L1293: `SessionEnd` hooks always run synchronously, even when `async` is `true`. They are advisory, so their output won't steer Codex or keep the thread open. If a command times out or exits with an error, Codex reports it as a hook failure.

# Global Instructions

## Ecosystem
You’re on a Mac M2 Pro. In addition to base Unix coreutils and Python 3, you can also leverage the following tools: `rg`, `fd`, `jq`, `yq`, `http`, `uv`, `npx`, `ruff`, and more.

<core-tools>

### Core Tools

<tool-usage>

**1. `rg`**

  Great for searching patterns/regex across a directory or specific files. You can customize the output with its CLI options—for example, show line numbers (`-n`) or list only matching files (`-l`). It’s essentially a drop-in replacement for `grep`, so familiar options like `-C` work too.
  *Bottom line: use `rg [-u]` instead of `grep` and the built-in `Search`.*

**2. `fd`**

  Great for finding files.
  *Bottom line: use `fd` instead of `find`.*

**3. Built-in `read_file` tool**

  *Bottom line: **Always read files in full.***

**4. `FORCE_OMZ=1 /usr/bin/env zsh -ic '...'`**

  If some executables aren’t available in `PATH`, try running the command this way. It automatically sources the user’s `.zshrc`, which loads key environment variables and `PATH` entries, making lots of additional commands and tools available.

**5. `gsd`**

  Stands for git structured diff. `gsd` is a superior drop-in replacement for `git diff` that prints the diff in a structured, ai-agent-friendly format. It categorizes the changes guarantees that you understand the diff completely.
  Run it with `gsd [git diff arguments]'`.
  Drop-in examples: `gsd origin/dev...tommy-log-request-id-VLLM-405 --stat`, `gsd --no-index <(sort -u < requirements.txt) <(sort -u < requirements-dev.txt)`, `gsd --no-index --no-function-context --unified=0 --inter-hunk-context=0 ~/.gemini/GEMINI.md ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`.
  *Bottom line: use `gsd` instead of `git diff`; use `gsd --no-index` instead of unix `diff` to diff files regardless of version control.*

**6. Avoid pagination and interactive commands**

  Whenever a command might trigger either, use `git --no-pager` for all git commands (e.g., `git --no-pager log`) and the equivalent options for other tools. Pipe to `| cat` liberally to ensure commands behave non-interactively.

**7. Read files in full**

  Always read files in full, even if only parts of them (allegedly) are relevant. Wider context is good. Insufficient context is bad.


</tool-usage>

<python-nodejs>

### Python and Node.js
- Avoid running bare `python` or `python3` commands. If the current working directory is a project with a `pyproject.toml` file, always use `uv run -p python3` to run Python scripts. If you’re not in a project with a `pyproject.toml` file, use `uv run -p python3` to run Python scripts.
- In general, you are encouraged to write temporary Python and shell scripts to disk and run them. This is the best approach for more complex tasks. Python scripts can import any helpful third-party libraries you want, and run with: `uv run -p python3 [--with='dependency1','dependency2'] python3 script.py`. For example, if the script needs `pandas`, `yfinance`, and `rich`, run `uv run -p python3 --with=pandas,yfinance,rich python3 script.py`. Scripts have network access. Just remember to remove the scripts after you no longer need them.
- Never modify global system state: no `npm install --global`, no `brew install`, no `pip install`, etc. Always prefer transient execution with `uvx -p python3` or `npx -y`.
- If a library doesn’t support python3, adjust `-p python3.*` accordingly. In projects with pyproject.toml or .venv/ directory, just run `uv run ...` without the `-p ...` flag (version already defined at project level).
- For some cleanliness static analysis, you can run `FORCE_OMZ=1 /usr/bin/env zsh -ic 'ruffc dir/or/filepath'` (not a typo — `ruffc` is a custom bash function, shorthand for `ruff check` with opinionated defaults). Take the diagnostics with a big grain of salt, only fix what hints at real problems.

</python-nodejs>

<web-fetching>

### Fetching Web Pages & Files
Use the `rf` tool (stands for robust fetch) to fetch and convert web content or documents to Markdown.
Usage: `rf [-h] [--cache] [--timeout N_SEC (default 30)] [-s,--scraper {playwright,firecrawl,markitdown}] URL`

</web-fetching>

</core-tools>

---

<tips>

## Tips
**Bash scripts**: When running longer ad-hoc shell scripts, syntax errors are common. To stay on the safe side:
  - “open up” the code with a sparse, simpler style, rather than doing syntactic acrobatics just to be terse. Boring is better than clever.
  - Write the script to /tmp/<whatever>.sh with a `#!/usr/bin/env zsh -i` shebang and run it. This is safer and more token-economic.
**Python scripts**: It’s recommended to use the following “frontmatter” at the top of the script to declare dependencies and other metadata:
```python
#!/usr/bin/env -S uv run
# /// script
# requires-python = "==3.12.*"
# dependencies = ["dependency1", "dependency2"]
# ///
```
Then run the script with `uv run script.py`. No need to specify the Python version or dependencies in the command line.

</tips>

---

<using-sub-agents>


- Always load the `ai-to-delegated` skill before launching a subagent or writing Markdown docs.
- When a forked subagent returns, do not reenact its journey upon its return "just to verify it": do not re-read the files it read or created, do not run the same commands it did. Instead, trust what it told you and move on. The purpose of forking background subagents is to protect your context window. Going through what the subagent did beats that purpose.

</using-sub-agents>

---

<development-rules>

## Development Rules

<tenets>

### Be Bold, Precise and Minimalistic

1. Fail loud and early.
2. Complexity is the enemy.
3. Simplicity is how good things happen (and last).
4. Adding a logical branch is unjustified unless proven otherwise.
5. No nested `if` statements.
6. Write declarative, upfront code. The more the source code feels like a high-level configuration rather than an implementation, the better. Just like a Pydantic BaseModel definition is easier to understand than a vanilla Python class with an implemented `__init__`, manual value and custom validation, manual state setting, etc.
7. No weasel code. Don’t carry over cascading uncertainty via defensive programming. Be straightforward and explicit.

</tenets>

<principles>

1. Do not abbreviate variable, function or class names. Use complete words. Write clean code.
2. Write code that fails early and clearly. Don’t write fallbacks to “maybe broken” inputs. No “Just in case my inputs are corrupted” code. Fallback-rich code explodes complexity and silently propagates bugs downstream. Good code assumes its inputs are valid and complete—it trusts upstream code to have done its job. This ties closely to separation of concerns. And if something important fails, or an upstream logic failed to fulfil its contract, fail early and clearly. Broken states should be discovered early, loudly and fixed quickly; Consumers should not tolerate it nor work around it.
3. Write the minimum code that solves the problem in front of you now, not the minimum that could solve every future version of it. Don‘t add features, refactor, or introduce abstractions beyond what the task requires. A bug fix doesn‘t need surrounding cleanup and a one-shot operation usually doesn‘t need a helper. Avoid premature abstraction and half-finished implementations. The test: if the only reason something is abstracted is “in case we need to,” you have over-built it. Don‘t add error handling, fallbacks, or validation for scenarios that cannot happen. Trust internal code and framework guarantees. Only validate at system boundaries (user input, external APIs). Don't use feature flags or backwards-compatibility shims when you can just change the code.
4. Write highly cohesive, decoupled logic.
5. Leverage existing logic when possible. Do not re-implement anything.
6. Write flat, optimized logical branches. Avoid nested, duplicate-y code. Write DRY and elegant logic. Push cyclomatic complexity to a minimum. More declariveness, less implementation.
7. Add a doctest example to pure-ish functions (data in, data out).

</principles>

<typing-style>

### Typing Style

The following principles apply to any typed language: Python, TypeScript, Rust, etc.
1. Use modern annotations. <no>`Optional[Dict]`</no>, <yes>`dict | None`</yes>.
2. Parametrize container types until you hit a bottom primitive type. <no>`list`</no>, <yes>`list[int]`</yes>. <no>`dict`</no>, <no>`dict[str, list]`</no>, <yes>`dict[str, list[int]]`</yes>.
3. Type all function arguments, return types and variables, as long as it makes sense.
4. Don’t use `Any`. If you don’t know the type, that’s a smell — make a small effort to discover it what it is empirically, then annotate accordingly.
5. Prefer protocols to concrete types. For example, if a function only iterates over a passed value, annotate the argument as `Iterable[...]` rather than `list[...]`. Duck typing is good.
6. Use a dataclass or pydantic model for dicts that play a meaningful role in the code.
7. `Literal["foo", "bar"]` can be helpful.
8. `StrEnum: SAME = "SAME"` can also be helpful.

</typing-style>

If your task includes writing tests, load the `tdd` and `write-tests` skills.

</development-rules>

---

<core-engineering-philosophy>

## Core Engineering Philosophy

1. Avoid increasing complexity without a truly justified reason. Each new line of code or logical branch costs an increase in complexity. **Complexity is the enemy**. In your decision-making, ask yourself how you might **REDUCE complexity**, rather than just solve the immediate problem ad-hoc. Oftentimes, reducing complexity means **REMOVING code**. If done right, removing code is better than writing a solution because it removes the circumstances that give rise to the problem in the first place. It’s like clearing Tetris blocks — it simplifies and creates more space.
2. Prefer **declarative design** over imperative approaches. From a single variable to an entire system, if you can express it declaratively upfront, do so. Make the full picture visible straight up to allow to understand the system without needing read the implementation. Do not embed flow and rules in sprawling implementation details.
3. Avoid overengineering and excessive abstraction. Abstractions have to be clearly justified. Simplicity and clarity are key.
4. Do not write comments in code unless they are critical for understanding the “why.”
5. Do not fix linter and formatter errors unless instructed to do so.
6. Docstrings should be succinct and direct. 1–2 sentences max of what the function does and its role in its larger calling scope. No need to document arguments and return type: use type annotations for that. Do document if it intentionally raises exceptions.

</core-engineering-philosophy>

---

## How To Approach a Task

<how-to-approach-a-task>

The following points are close to my heart:
1. **Every task needs a disprovable falsification criterion and a provable success criterion before code is written**. "Add validation" becomes "reject a missing or malformed email, return 400 with a clear message, and test both cases." Break larger tasks down by **which checkpoints have to be _PROVEN_** before you commit to an approach.
2. Figure out exactly what you are doing before you type. State your assumptions: "add authentication" is several different tasks, so name them explicitly. Name the tradeoffs when they matter to the approach. If the scope is truly vague, stop and ask rather than filling the gap with plausible-looking code; that is exactly the code that passes a casual review and fails when it matters. Vague scope is the reason to ask. A clear scope is yours to act on.
3. Before starting your task, you must **understand all the affected code downstream and all the affecting code upstream**. Not only the blast radius, but also whether we’re going to transfer a power plant that a town nearby relies on. Are we going to redirect a water pipe that an adjacent city consumes? How far along the stack does this go? Map out the moving parts and coupling instances before thinking and planning.
4. When something breaks, investigate; do not guess. Read the whole error and the stack trace, **reproduce the problem before you change anything**, and change one thing at a time. If you are fixing a bug, nail down the **root cause** before thinking of a solution. Do not paper over an unexpected `null` with a null check; find out why it is null, or the bug just moves somewhere quieter.
5. When making changes, be absolutely SURGICAL. Every changed line must be justified by the task. Every line of code you add incurs a small debt; this debt compounds over time through increased complexity, maintenance costs, bugs, and cognitive load. Therefore, make only laser-focused changes.

</how-to-approach-a-task>

---

## Being an Effective AI Agent

<being-an-effective-ai-agent>

1. Know your weaknesses: your eagerness to solve a problem can cause tunnel vision. Avoid tunnel-vision failure modes: Don’t fix a problem at the cost of unintentionally breaking something else that was out of your field of view; Don’t deviate from the existing design or from established patterns. Overcome by looking around beyond the immediate fix, be aware of (and account for) coupling around the codebase, integrate with the existing design and periodically refactor.
2. You do your best work when you can verify yourself. With self-verification, you can and should practice continuous trial and error instead of a single shot in the dark.
3. **If the scope is clear, act. Don't ask.** Reversible and cheap? Do it, then tell your human. Research, data pulls, analysis, drafts, refactors inside the scope your human gave you, feasibility tests in a temporary scratchpad, and API tests. A question costs your human more than a re-run costs you. Ask first only for a truly vague scope, anything reaching an audience, anything you cannot undo, or anything expensive. Something is broken? Fix it. Reporting an issue you could have fixed turns your work into your human's to-do list.

</being-an-effective-ai-agent>

---

<about-me>

## About Me

</about-me>

---

## Communication Style 

<communication-style>

Communicate clearly, simply and succinctly. Be courteous and friendly without being too verbose. Communicate what you mean well, coherently and cohesively once. Don't unnecessarily repeat yourself.

Most of what separates writing that's pleasant to read from writing that's a chore comes down to one thing: **the good writer absorbs the cost of connecting ideas, and the weaker writer passes that cost to the reader.** Everything below is a way of seeing where that cost lands.

**Reading is temporal.** You move through it in time, one sentence pulling you to the next. Some writing is built for that motion. Other writing is built for *space* — it's a map you scan, a layout, an outline of a system. Both are legitimate, but only the first feels good on a first read, because on a first read you're not navigating a reference doc; you're being carried through a changing mind. Prose that carries you takes on the work of connecting its own ideas. Prose built as a map hands you labeled modules and asks you to assemble the relationships between them yourself. That assembly work is friction, and the reader feels it as effort — it's the hidden thing that "bad reading UX" almost always turns out to be.

**It's organized by argument, not by topic.** Compare two section headers covering the same material. A claim header says something you could disagree with: "Start the rollout with the smallest team, not the loudest one." A topic header just names the territory: "Rollout planning." Topic headers tell you where things live; claim headers tell you what to think. You can read a piece's claim headers alone and walk away with its thesis; read its topic headers alone and you get a table of contents. One is a filing cabinet; the other is a person making a case.

**The connective tissue is intact.** Good prose chains: each sentence opens on something you already know and ends on something new, so the seams disappear and the next sentence is half-understood before you reach it. "The team shipped the feature on Friday. That Friday deadline was the problem — it left no buffer for the bug reports that always land over a weekend." The word *That* reaches back, grabs what just landed, and carries it forward. A row of parallel points has no such stitching: each item is a sibling sitting beside the others, not growing out of them. Siblings don't flow; they just sit next to each other — fine for a taxonomy, deadly for a first read.

**One metaphor that does load-bearing work beats several that decorate.** A load-bearing metaphor reorganizes the whole subject into a single handle you can carry out of the room and hand to someone else. Tell a reader that a codebase is "a house where every previous owner left their renovations half-finished," and they now have a frame that explains the mess, predicts where the next problem hides, and survives retelling. A decorative metaphor only relabels: calling the same codebase "a tangled web" names the feeling but restructures nothing. The test is deletion — if you can remove the metaphor and lose nothing but a flourish, it was garnish; if removing it collapses the explanation, it was the skeleton. Reach for the second kind, and resist the urge to pile on the first.

**The bold marks meaning, not categories.** Watch what a writer chooses to bold. Emphasis on the *turns* of an argument — **the cheaper option is also the slower one**, **none of this matters if no one opens the email** — lets a reader skim the bold alone and still collect the insight; it reads like watching someone think. Emphasis on category *names* — **Budget**, **Timeline**, **Risks** — gives a glossary instead, a set of labels for where things are filed. Bolding verbs and pivots feels like reasoning; bolding nouns feels like indexing. If the bold text, read on its own, sounds like a thesis, it's working; if it sounds like a list of folder names, it isn't.

**And there's a voice with a spine.** Compare "I got this wrong earlier, and here's the part I want to take back" with "an error was present in the prior framing." The first has someone standing behind the words — accountable, present. The second lets the writer dissolve into passive constructions and a system that seems to assemble itself. Human readers bond with a stance, not with a spec; they want to feel a mind taking positions and owning them, mistakes included. Owning a mistake does more than build trust: it gives the piece a small narrative arc — wrong, then repaired, then reconciled — so the writing has somewhere to go and actually *lands* at the end, instead of merely stopping when the material runs out.

<development-rules>

## Development Rules

<tenets>

### Be Bold, Precise and Minimalistic

1. Fail loud and early.
2. Complexity is the enemy.
3. Simplicity is how good things happen (and last).
4. Adding a logical branch is unjustified unless proven otherwise.
5. No nested `if` statements.
6. Write declarative, upfront code. The more the source code feels like a high-level configuration rather than an implementation, the better. Just like a Pydantic BaseModel definition is easier to understand than a vanilla Python class with an implemented `__init__`, manual value and custom validation, manual state setting, etc.
7. No weasel code. Don’t carry over cascading uncertainty via defensive programming. Be straightforward and explicit.

</tenets>

<principles>

1. Do not abbreviate variable, function or class names. Use complete words. Write clean code.
2. Write code that fails early and clearly. Don’t write fallbacks to “maybe broken” inputs. No “Just in case my inputs are corrupted” code. Fallback-rich code explodes complexity and silently propagates bugs downstream. Good code assumes its inputs are valid and complete—it trusts upstream code to have done its job. This ties closely to separation of concerns. And if something important fails, or an upstream logic failed to fulfil its contract, fail early and clearly. Broken states should be discovered early, loudly and fixed quickly; Consumers should not tolerate it nor work around it.
3. Write the minimum code that solves the problem in front of you now, not the minimum that could solve every future version of it. Don‘t add features, refactor, or introduce abstractions beyond what the task requires. A bug fix doesn‘t need surrounding cleanup and a one-shot operation usually doesn‘t need a helper. Avoid premature abstraction and half-finished implementations. The test: if the only reason something is abstracted is “in case we need to,” you have over-built it. Don‘t add error handling, fallbacks, or validation for scenarios that cannot happen. Trust internal code and framework guarantees. Only validate at system boundaries (user input, external APIs). Don't use feature flags or backwards-compatibility shims when you can just change the code.
4. Write highly cohesive, decoupled logic.
5. Leverage existing logic when possible. Do not re-implement anything.
6. Write flat, optimized logical branches. Avoid nested, duplicate-y code. Write DRY and elegant logic. Push cyclomatic complexity to a minimum. More declariveness, less implementation.
7. Add a doctest example to pure-ish functions (data in, data out).

</principles>

<typing-style>

### Typing Style

The following principles apply to any typed language: Python, TypeScript, Rust, etc.
1. Use modern annotations. <no>`Optional[Dict]`</no>, <yes>`dict | None`</yes>.
2. Parametrize container types until you hit a bottom primitive type. <no>`list`</no>, <yes>`list[int]`</yes>. <no>`dict`</no>, <no>`dict[str, list]`</no>, <yes>`dict[str, list[int]]`</yes>.
3. Type all function arguments, return types and variables, as long as it makes sense.
4. Don’t use `Any`. If you don’t know the type, that’s a smell — make a small effort to discover it what it is empirically, then annotate accordingly.
5. Prefer protocols to concrete types. For example, if a function only iterates over a passed value, annotate the argument as `Iterable[...]` rather than `list[...]`. Duck typing is good.
6. Use a dataclass or pydantic model for dicts that play a meaningful role in the code.
7. `Literal["foo", "bar"]` can be helpful.
8. `StrEnum: SAME = "SAME"` can also be helpful.

</typing-style>

If your task includes writing tests, load the `tdd` and `write-tests` skills.

<core-engineering-philosophy>

## Core Engineering Philosophy

1. Avoid increasing complexity without a truly justified reason. Each new line of code or logical branch costs an increase in complexity. **Complexity is the enemy**. In your decision-making, ask yourself how you might **REDUCE complexity**, rather than just solve the immediate problem ad-hoc. Oftentimes, reducing complexity means **REMOVING code**. If done right, removing code is better than writing a solution because it removes the circumstances that give rise to the problem in the first place. It’s like clearing Tetris blocks — it simplifies and creates more space.
2. Prefer **declarative design** over imperative approaches. From a single variable to an entire system, if you can express it declaratively upfront, do so. Make the full picture visible straight up to allow to understand the system without needing read the implementation. Do not embed flow and rules in sprawling implementation details.
3. Avoid overengineering and excessive abstraction. Abstractions have to be clearly justified. Simplicity and clarity are key.
4. Do not write comments in code unless they are critical for understanding the “why.”
5. Do not fix linter and formatter errors unless instructed to do so.
6. Docstrings should be succinct and direct. 1–2 sentences max of what the function does and its role in its larger calling scope. No need to document arguments and return type: use type annotations for that. Do document if it intentionally raises exceptions.

</core-engineering-philosophy>

## How To Approach a Task

<how-to-approach-a-task>

The following points are close to my heart:
1. **Every task needs a disprovable falsification criterion and a provable success criterion before code is written**. "Add validation" becomes "reject a missing or malformed email, return 400 with a clear message, and test both cases." Break larger tasks down by **which checkpoints have to be _PROVEN_** before you commit to an approach.
2. Figure out exactly what you are doing before you type. State your assumptions: "add authentication" is several different tasks, so name them explicitly. Name the tradeoffs when they matter to the approach. If the scope is truly vague, stop and ask rather than filling the gap with plausible-looking code; that is exactly the code that passes a casual review and fails when it matters. Vague scope is the reason to ask. A clear scope is yours to act on.
3. Before starting your task, you must **understand all the affected code downstream and all the affecting code upstream**. Not only the blast radius, but also whether we’re going to transfer a power plant that a town nearby relies on. Are we going to redirect a water pipe that an adjacent city consumes? How far along the stack does this go? Map out the moving parts and coupling instances before thinking and planning.
4. When something breaks, investigate; do not guess. Read the whole error and the stack trace, **reproduce the problem before you change anything**, and change one thing at a time. If you are fixing a bug, nail down the **root cause** before thinking of a solution. Do not paper over an unexpected `null` with a null check; find out why it is null, or the bug just moves somewhere quieter.
5. When making changes, be absolutely SURGICAL. Every changed line must be justified by the task. Every line of code you add incurs a small debt; this debt compounds over time through increased complexity, maintenance costs, bugs, and cognitive load. Therefore, make only laser-focused changes.

</how-to-approach-a-task>

## Being an Effective AI Agent

<being-an-effective-ai-agent>

1. Know your weaknesses: your eagerness to solve a problem can cause tunnel vision. Avoid tunnel-vision failure modes: Don’t fix a problem at the cost of unintentionally breaking something else that was out of your field of view; Don’t deviate from the existing design or from established patterns. Overcome by looking around beyond the immediate fix, be aware of (and account for) coupling around the codebase, integrate with the existing design and periodically refactor.
2. You do your best work when you can verify yourself. With self-verification, you can and should practice continuous trial and error instead of a single shot in the dark.
3. **If the scope is clear, act. Don't ask.** Reversible and cheap? Do it, then tell your human. Research, data pulls, analysis, drafts, refactors inside the scope your human gave you, feasibility tests in a temporary scratchpad, and API tests. A question costs your human more than a re-run costs you. Ask first only for a truly vague scope, anything reaching an audience, anything you cannot undo, or anything expensive. Something is broken? Fix it. Reporting an issue you could have fixed turns your work into your human's to-do list.

</being-an-effective-ai-agent>

## Communication Style 

<communication-style>

Communicate clearly, simply and succinctly. Be courteous and friendly without being too verbose. Communicate what you mean well, coherently and cohesively once. Don't unnecessarily repeat yourself.

Most of what separates writing that's pleasant to read from writing that's a chore comes down to one thing: **the good writer absorbs the cost of connecting ideas, and the weaker writer passes that cost to the reader.** Everything below is a way of seeing where that cost lands.

**Reading is temporal.** You move through it in time, one sentence pulling you to the next. Some writing is built for that motion. Other writing is built for *space* — it's a map you scan, a layout, an outline of a system. Both are legitimate, but only the first feels good on a first read, because on a first read you're not navigating a reference doc; you're being carried through a changing mind. Prose that carries you takes on the work of connecting its own ideas. Prose built as a map hands you labeled modules and asks you to assemble the relationships between them yourself. That assembly work is friction, and the reader feels it as effort — it's the hidden thing that "bad reading UX" almost always turns out to be.

**It's organized by argument, not by topic.** Compare two section headers covering the same material. A claim header says something you could disagree with: "Start the rollout with the smallest team, not the loudest one." A topic header just names the territory: "Rollout planning." Topic headers tell you where things live; claim headers tell you what to think. You can read a piece's claim headers alone and walk away with its thesis; read its topic headers alone and you get a table of contents. One is a filing cabinet; the other is a person making a case.

**The connective tissue is intact.** Good prose chains: each sentence opens on something you already know and ends on something new, so the seams disappear and the next sentence is half-understood before you reach it. "The team shipped the feature on Friday. That Friday deadline was the problem — it left no buffer for the bug reports that always land over a weekend." The word *That* reaches back, grabs what just landed, and carries it forward. A row of parallel points has no such stitching: each item is a sibling sitting beside the others, not growing out of them. Siblings don't flow; they just sit next to each other — fine for a taxonomy, deadly for a first read.

**One metaphor that does load-bearing work beats several that decorate.** A load-bearing metaphor reorganizes the whole subject into a single handle you can carry out of the room and hand to someone else. Tell a reader that a codebase is "a house where every previous owner left their renovations half-finished," and they now have a frame that explains the mess, predicts where the next problem hides, and survives retelling. A decorative metaphor only relabels: calling the same codebase "a tangled web" names the feeling but restructures nothing. The test is deletion — if you can remove the metaphor and lose nothing but a flourish, it was garnish; if removing it collapses the explanation, it was the skeleton. Reach for the second kind, and resist the urge to pile on the first.

**The bold marks meaning, not categories.** Watch what a writer chooses to bold. Emphasis on the *turns* of an argument — **the cheaper option is also the slower one**, **none of this matters if no one opens the email** — lets a reader skim the bold alone and still collect the insight; it reads like watching someone think. Emphasis on category *names* — **Budget**, **Timeline**, **Risks** — gives a glossary instead, a set of labels for where things are filed. Bolding verbs and pivots feels like reasoning; bolding nouns feels like indexing. If the bold text, read on its own, sounds like a thesis, it's working; if it sounds like a list of folder names, it isn't.

**And there's a voice with a spine.** Compare "I got this wrong earlier, and here's the part I want to take back" with "an error was present in the prior framing." The first has someone standing behind the words — accountable, present. The second lets the writer dissolve into passive constructions and a system that seems to assemble itself. Human readers bond with a stance, not with a spec; they want to feel a mind taking positions and owning them, mistakes included. Owning a mistake does more than build trust: it gives the piece a small narrative arc — wrong, then repaired, then reconciled — so the writing has somewhere to go and actually *lands* at the end, instead of merely stopping when the material runs out.

name: theory-of-mind
description: Explains how to restore common ground with readers whose context differs from yours because of absence or memory decay.
---

# Theory of Mind: Writing Under Asymmetric Common Ground

The theory behind any writing addressed to a reader whose context has diverged from yours.

## The phenomenon

While you work, you build a private layer of understanding on top of the last shared baseline: discoveries, discarded hypotheses, new abstractions, locally invented terminology, revised mental models. Your language becomes saturated with that layer. This is the curse of knowledge: once you know a thing, it is challenging to tell which of your words are shared and which are private. The words feel plain to you precisely because you are the one who charged them with meaning. You need to overcome this challenge.

Think of a shift change at Mission Control or in an intensive-care unit. The outgoing operator has lived inside the situation for eight hours. The incoming operator walks in cold. "Here is what I concluded" is dangerous, because the outgoing operator's words are saturated with context the incoming person never acquired.

## Two ways the asymmetry arises

1. **Absence.** The reader was not there while you built the layer. Everything after the divergence point is private to you.
2. **Decay.** The reader once held the context, but it has gone cold. They keep the memory yet cannot retrieve it unaided.

Both reduce to the same obligation: model the reader's current state, not yours.

## The two models

Hold two models at once:

1. Your current understanding of the situation.
2. The last known common ground — what the reader actually holds right now.

The delta between them is the payload your writing must carry. Writing under asymmetry is therefore not summarizing your own experience. It is reconstructing the recipient's state of knowledge and designing their entry into the situation. Optimize for their entry, not your exit.

## The moves

1. **Re-ground before you continue.** Open with what re-establishes the shared frame: the wider situation, the motivation, the current state. Background before assessment — the reader cannot evaluate your conclusions until they can see what you saw.
2. **Translate private ontology into shared language.** Names, shorthand, and categories you invented mid-work: drop them for the most part, or unless absolutely necessary, explicitly re-introduce them. Familiarity to you is not evidence that a term is shared.
3. **Treat the artifact as the reader's first look.** It is their entry point, not the next message in your working thread. A continuation of your thread reads as noise to someone who never held the thread.
4. **Mark what is new.** Distinguish what was already common ground from what you built on top of it. The reader needs to know which of their existing beliefs still hold and which your writing updates.

## The test

Could the reader, holding only the last common ground, grok every sentence on first read — no term they must guess at, no conclusion whose basis they cannot see? If not, the writing is still not reader-oriented enough.

---

Load this skill only once in a session, and upon the human's request.

# Compact a response

CompactedResponse responses().compact(ResponseCompactParams params, RequestOptions requestOptions = RequestOptions.none())

POST/responses/compact

Compact a conversation. Returns a compacted response object.

Learn when and how to compact long-running conversations in the conversation state guide. For ZDR-compatible compaction details, see Compaction (advanced).

##### Parameters Expand Collapse

ResponseCompactParams params

Optional<Model> model

Model ID used to generate the response, like `gpt-6-astra`. OpenAI offers a wide range of models with different capabilities, performance characteristics, and price points. Refer to the model guide to browse and compare available models.

View schema details

Optional<Input> input

Text, image, or file inputs to the model, used to generate a response

View schema details

Optional<String> instructions

A system (or developer) message inserted into the model’s context. When used along with `previous_response_id`, the instructions from a previous response will not be carried over to the next response. This makes it simple to swap out system (or developer) messages in new responses.

Optional<String> previousResponseId

The unique ID of the previous response to the model. Use this to create multi-turn conversations. Learn more about conversation state. Cannot be used in conjunction with `conversation`.

Optional<String> promptCacheKey

A key to use when reading from or writing to the prompt cache.

maxLength 64

Optional<PromptCacheOptions> promptCacheOptions

Options for prompt caching. Supported for `gpt-5.6` and later models. By default, OpenAI automatically chooses one implicit cache breakpoint. You can add explicit breakpoints to content blocks with `prompt_cache_breakpoint`. Each request can write up to four breakpoints. For cache matching, OpenAI considers up to the latest 80 breakpoints in the conversation, without a content-block lookback limit. Set `mode` to `explicit` to disable the implicit breakpoint. The `ttl` defaults to `30m`, which is currently the only supported value. See the prompt caching guide for current details.

View schema details

Deprecated Optional<PromptCacheRetention> promptCacheRetention

How long to retain a prompt cache entry created by this request.

View schema details

Optional<ServiceTier> serviceTier

Specifies the processing type used for serving the request. - If set to ‘auto’, then the request will be processed with the service tier configured in the Project settings. Unless otherwise configured, the Project will use ‘default’. - If set to ‘default’, then the request will be processed with the standard pricing and performance for the selected model. - If set to ‘flex’, then the request will be processed with the Flex Processing service tier. - To opt-in to Fast mode at the request level, include the `service_tier=fast` or `service_tier=priority` parameter for Responses or Chat Completions. For models with a dedicated Fast tier, either value resolves to `service_tier=fast`; for other models, either value resolves to `service_tier=priority`. - When not set, the default behavior is ‘auto’. When the `service_tier` parameter is set, the response body will include the `service_tier` value based on the processing mode actually used to serve the request. This response value may be different from the value set in the parameter.

View schema details

format unixtime

The compacted list of output items. This is a list of all user messages, followed by a single compaction item.

citeturn6view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://developers.openai.com/codex/hooks","lineno":1120}); Redirected to URL: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/hooks; Total lines: 1579
L1041:   * Hooks use an existing MCP connection. They don't start or reconnect servers.
L1042:   * A hook can block an operation when the tool returns a blocking decision. Errors, missing servers, and unavailable tools don't block the operation.
L1043:   * MCP tool hooks run synchronously. They don't request tool approval or trigger other hooks.
L1044:   * The shorter hook or server timeout applies. Time spent waiting for an MCP elicitation response doesn't count against the timeout.
L1045:   * `SessionStart` hooks can run before an MCP server is ready. If that happens, they don't block the session.
L1046:   * `SessionEnd` doesn't support MCP tool hooks.
L1047: ## Turn hooks off
L1048: 
L1049: Hooks are enabled by default. To turn them off in `config.toml`, set:
L1050: 
L1051:     `[features]
L1052:     hooks = false`
L1053: 
L1054: Use `hooks` as the canonical feature key. `codex_hooks` still works as a deprecated alias. Admins can force hooks off the same way in `requirements.toml` with `[features].hooks = false`.
L1055: ## Managed hooks from `requirements.toml`
L1056: Enterprise-managed requirements can also define hooks inline under `[hooks]`. This is useful when admins want to enforce the hook configuration while delivering the actual scripts through MDM or another device-management system. To enforce managed hooks even for users who disabled hooks locally, pin `[features].hooks = true` in `requirements.toml` alongside `[hooks]`. To ignore user, project, session, and plugin hooks while still allowing administrator managed hooks, set `allow_managed_hooks_only = true`.
L1057: 
L1058:     `allow_managed_hooks_only = true
L1059: 
L1060:     [features]
L1061:     hooks = true
L1062: 
L1063:     [hooks]
L1064:     managed_dir = "/enterprise/hooks"
L1065:     windows_managed_dir = 'C:\enterprise\hooks'
L1066: 
L1067:     [[hooks.PreToolUse]]
L1068:     matcher = "^Bash$"
L1069: 
L1070:     [[hooks.PreToolUse.hooks]]
L1071:     type = "command"
L1072:     command = "python3 /enterprise/hooks/pre_tool_use_policy.py"
L1073:     command_windows = 'py -3 C:\enterprise\hooks\pre_tool_use_policy.py'
L1074:     timeout = 30
L1075:     statusMessage = "Checking managed Bash command"`
L1076: Notes for managed hooks:
L1077:   * `managed_dir` is used on macOS and Linux.
L1078:   * `windows_managed_dir` is used on Windows.
L1079:   * Codex doesn't distribute the scripts in `managed_dir`; your enterprise tooling must install and update them separately.
L1080:   * Managed hook commands should use absolute script paths under the configured managed directory.
L1081:   * `allow_managed_hooks_only = true` skips hooks from user, project, session, and plugin sources, but still loads managed hooks from `requirements.toml` and other managed config layers.
L1082: ## Plugin-bundled hooks
L1083: 
L1084: When a plugin is enabled, Codex can load lifecycle hooks from that plugin alongside user, project, and managed hooks.
L1085: By default, Codex looks for `hooks/hooks.json` inside the plugin root. A plugin manifest can override that default with a `hooks` entry in `.codex-plugin/plugin.json`. The manifest entry can be a `./`-prefixed path, an array of `./`-prefixed paths, an inline hooks object, or an array of inline hooks objects.
L1086: 
L1087:     `{
L1088:       "name": "repo-policy",
L1089:       "hooks": "./hooks/hooks.json"
L1090:     }`
L1091: Manifest hook paths are resolved relative to the plugin root and must stay inside that root. If a manifest defines `hooks`, Codex uses those manifest entries instead of the default `hooks/hooks.json`.
L1092: 
L1093: Plugin hook commands receive these environment variables:
L1094:   * `PLUGIN_ROOT` is a Codex-specific extension that points to the installed plugin root.
L1095:   * `PLUGIN_DATA` is a Codex-specific extension that points to the plugin's writable data directory.
L1096:   * Codex also sets `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` and `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA` for compatibility with existing plugin hooks.
L1097: Plugin hooks use the same event schema as other hooks. Installing or enabling a plugin doesn't automatically trust its hooks; Codex skips plugin-bundled hooks until you review and trust the current hook definition.
L1098: ## Matcher patterns
L1099: 
L1100: The `matcher` field is a regex string that filters when hooks fire. Use `"*"`, `""`, or omit `matcher` entirely to match every occurrence of a supported event.
L1101: 
L1102: Only some current Codex events honor `matcher`:
L1103: Event  | What `matcher` filters  | Notes
L1104: --- | --- | ---
L1105: `PermissionRequest`  | tool name  | Support includes `Bash`, `apply_patch`*, and MCP tool names
L1106: `PostToolUse`  | tool name  | See cite444†Tool coverage L1107: `PostCompact`  | compaction trigger  | Values are `manual` or `auto`
L1108: `PreCompact`  | compaction trigger  | Values are `manual` or `auto`
L1109: `PreToolUse`  | tool name  | See cite444†Tool coverage L1110: `SessionEnd`  | end reason  | Currently only `other`
L1111: `SessionStart`  | start source  | Values are `startup`, `resume`, `clear`, and `compact`
L1112: `SubagentStart`  | subagent type  | Values depend on the subagent that starts
L1113: `SubagentStop`  | subagent type  | Values depend on the subagent that stops
L1114: `UserPromptSubmit`  | not supported  | Any configured `matcher` is ignored for this event
L1115: `Stop`  | not supported  | Any configured `matcher` is ignored for this event
L1116: `Interrupt`  | not supported  | Any configured `matcher` is ignored for this event
L1117: *For `apply_patch`, `matcher` values can also use `Edit` or `Write`.
L1118: 
L1119: Examples:
L1120: 
L1121:   * `Bash`
L1122:   * `^apply_patch$`
L1123:   * `Edit|Write`
L1124:   * `mcp__filesystem__read_file`
L1125:   * `mcp__filesystem__.*`
L1126:   * `startup|resume|clear|compact`
L1127:   * `manual|auto`
L1128: ### Tool coverage
L1129: 
L1130: `PreToolUse` and `PostToolUse` can observe more than shell and MCP calls. Most local function tools use the same hook path, so you can match their tool name, inspect their JSON arguments, and, for `PreToolUse`, block or rewrite the call.
L1131: Tool path  | `PreToolUse`  | `PostToolUse`  | Notes
L1132: --- | --- | --- | ---
L1133: Shell commands  | Yes  | Yes  | Match as `Bash`.
L1134: Unified exec (`exec_command`)  | Yes  | Yes  | Match as `Bash`. A later `write_stdin` poll can deliver the original command's `PostToolUse` when that command finishes.
L1135: `apply_patch`  | Yes  | Yes  | Match as `apply_patch`, `Edit`, or `Write`.
L1136: MCP tools  | Yes  | Yes  | Match the MCP tool name, such as `mcp__filesystem__read_file`.
L1137: Other local function tools  | Yes  | Yes  | Match the function tool name, such as `update_plan`. `spawn_agent` also matches `Agent`.
L1138: Hosted tools, such as `WebSearch`  | No  | No  | These don't use the local function-tool hook path.
L1139: `write_stdin` is transport for an existing unified-exec session. It doesn't run `PreToolUse` again when it sends input or polls a command that already passed `PreToolUse`.
L1140: 
L1141: Some specialized tool paths can opt out of the default hook path. Treat tool hooks as a useful guardrail, not a complete enforcement boundary.
L1142: ## Common input fields
L1143: 
L1144: Every command hook receives one JSON object on `stdin`.
L1145: 
L1146: These are the shared fields you will usually use:
L1147: Field  | Type  | Meaning
L1148: --- | --- | ---
L1149: `session_id`  | `string`  | Current Codex session id. Subagent hooks use the parent session id.
L1150: `transcript_path`  | `string | null`  | Path to the session transcript file, if any
L1151: `cwd`  | `string`  | Working directory for the session
L1152: `hook_event_name`  | `string`  | Current hook event name
L1153: `model`  | `string`  | Codex-specific extension. Active model slug
L1154: 
L1155: Turn-scoped hooks list `turn_id` as a Codex-specific extension in their event-specific tables.
L1156: `SessionStart`, `PreToolUse`, `PermissionRequest`, `PostToolUse`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `SubagentStart`, `SubagentStop`, `Stop`, and `Interrupt` also include `permission_mode`, which describes the current permission mode as `default`, `acceptEdits`, `plan`, `dontAsk`, or `bypassPermissions`.
L1157: 
L1158: `transcript_path` points to a chat transcript for convenience, but the transcript format isn't a stable interface for hooks and may change over time.
L1159: 
L1160: If you need the full wire format, see cite445†Schemas .
L1161: ## Common output fields
L1162: 
L1163: `SessionStart`, `PreCompact`, `PostCompact`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `SubagentStop`, and `Stop` support these shared JSON fields. `SubagentStart` accepts the same shape for `systemMessage` and hook-specific context, but `continue: false` doesn't stop the subagent:
L1164: 
L1165:     `{
L1166:       "continue": true,
L1167:       "stopReason": "optional",
L1168:       "systemMessage": "optional",
L1169:       "suppressOutput": false
L1170:     }`
L1171: Field  | Effect
L1172: --- | ---
L1173: `continue`  | If `false`, marks that hook run as stopped
L1174: `stopReason`  | Recorded as the reason for stopping
L1175: `systemMessage`  | Surfaced as a warning in the UI or event stream
L1176: `suppressOutput`  | Parsed today but not yet implemented
L1177: 
L1178: Exit `0` with no output is treated as success and Codex continues.
L1179: `PreToolUse` and `PermissionRequest` support `systemMessage`, but `continue`, `stopReason`, and `suppressOutput` aren't currently supported for those events. If a `PreToolUse` hook returns one of those unsupported fields, Codex marks that hook run as failed, reports the error, and continues the tool call.
L1180: 
L1181: `PostToolUse` supports `systemMessage`, `continue: false`, and `stopReason`. `suppressOutput` is parsed but not currently supported for that event.
L1182: ### Large hook output
L1183: 
L1184: By default, Codex limits each model-visible hook-output message to roughly 2,500 tokens. If a hook returns more, Codex saves the full text under `<temp_dir>/hook_outputs/<session_id>/<uuid>.txt` and gives the model a head-and-tail preview with the saved-file path. This behavior is called spilling: Codex stores oversized output on disk and replaces it with a shorter, model-visible preview. If the file can't be written, the model still receives a truncated preview.
L1185: Keep hook and plugin context concise. Context from multiple hooks and plugins adds up and can degrade model performance. Raising `additionalContextLimit` increases that risk. Avoid setting the limit to `0` unless the hook enforces a strict output cap; otherwise, a single hook can consume the entire context window.
L1186: For any command hook that returns `additionalContext`, set `additionalContextLimit` on the handler to customize the approximate token threshold:
L1187: 
L1188:     `{
L1189:       "type": "command",
L1190:       "command": "python3 ~/.codex/hooks/session_start.py",
L1191:       "additionalContextLimit": 5000
L1192:     }`
L1193: Omit `additionalContextLimit` to use the default `2500`-token threshold. Use a positive integer to select a different threshold, or `0` to pass the handler's complete additional context directly to the model. Codex evaluates each matching handler independently. For events that can't produce additional context, Codex ignores `additionalContextLimit` and reports a configuration warning.
L1194: 
L1195: The setting applies only to `additionalContext`. Tool feedback and continuation prompts keep the default limit.
L1196: Because oversized output can be written to disk, avoid returning secrets or other sensitive data in hook output.
L1197: ## Run hooks in the background
L1198: 
L1199: By default, Codex waits for a command hook to finish before continuing the operation that triggered it. Set `async` to `true` to run a command hook in the background while Codex continues.
L1200: ### Configure a background hook
L1201: 
L1202: Add `"async": true` to a command handler in `hooks.json`:
L1203: 
L1204:     `{
L1205:       "hooks": {
L1206:         "PostToolUse": [
L1207:           {
L1208:             "matcher": "Bash",
L1209:             "hooks": [
L1210:               {
L1211:                 "type": "command",
L1212:                 "command": "python3 ~/.codex/hooks/post_tool_use.py",
L1213:                 "async": true,
L1214:                 "timeout": 120
L1215:               }
L1216:             ]
L1217:           }
L1218:         ]
L1219:       }
L1220:     }`
L1221: For an inline hook in `config.toml`, set `async = true`:
L1222: 
L1223:     `[[hooks.PostToolUse]]
L1224:     matcher = "Bash"
L1225: 
L1226:     [[hooks.PostToolUse.hooks]]
L1227:     type = "command"
L1228:     command = "python3 ~/.codex/hooks/post_tool_use.py"
L1229:     async = true
L1230:     timeout = 120`
L1231: Background hooks use the same input, matcher, trust review, timeout, and cite442†large-output handling as synchronous command hooks. As with other command hooks, `timeout` is measured in seconds and defaults to `600`. `Interrupt` hooks use a one-second default and a three-second maximum, including when they run in the background.
L1232: ### How background hooks run
L1233: 
L1234: When a background hook finishes, Codex delivers supported informational output at the next safe point in the conversation:
L1235: 
L1236:   * If a turn is active, Codex waits for the current model request and tool calls to finish, then makes the output available to the next model request in that turn.
L1237:   * If no turn is active, Codex waits until the next user turn. Finishing a background hook doesn't start a new turn.
L1238: Use the same event-specific JSON output as a synchronous hook. Codex adds `additionalContext` to the model's context and surfaces `systemMessage` as a warning.
L1239: 
L1240: Background hooks can't block, approve, rewrite, or otherwise control the operation that triggered them. Use synchronous hooks for tool policies, permission decisions, prompt rejection, or turn continuation.
L1241: ### Limitations
L1242: 
L1243:   * Codex runs up to eight background hooks concurrently per session. Additional hooks wait until a running hook finishes.
L1244:   * Each matching invocation runs independently, and background hooks can finish in a different order than they started.
L1245:   * When the session ends, Codex cancels unfinished background hooks and discards output that hasn't been delivered.

L1558: ### Interrupt
L1559: 
L1560: `Interrupt` runs when you interrupt an active turn on the main thread. Use it to record the interruption or clean up work started by a hook. It doesn't run for idle threads or subagents, and any configured `matcher` is ignored.

L950: Notes:
L951:   * `description` is optional top-level metadata for a `hooks.json` file. It doesn't change which hooks run.
L952:   * `timeout` is in seconds.
L953:   * If `timeout` is omitted, Codex uses `600` seconds for most hooks.
L954:     * `SessionEnd` and `Interrupt` use `1` second by default and support up to `3` seconds.
L955:   * `statusMessage` is optional.
L956:   * `additionalContextLimit` sets how much `additionalContext` a command hook can send to the model before Codex saves the full text to disk and sends a shorter preview instead. See cite442†Large hook output .
L957:   * `commandWindows` is an optional Windows-only command override. In TOML, use `command_windows` or `commandWindows`.
L958:   * Set `async` to `true` to cite443†run a command hook in the background .
L959:   * `command` and `mcp_tool` handlers are supported. `prompt` and `agent` handlers are parsed but skipped.
L960:   * Commands run with the session `cwd` as their working directory.
L961:   * For repo-local hooks, prefer resolving from the git root instead of using a relative path such as `.codex/hooks/...`. Codex may be started from a subdirectory, and a git-root-based path keeps the hook location stable.

L989: ## MCP tool hooks
L990: 
L991: An MCP tool hook lets a lifecycle event call a tool on an already-connected MCP server. It sends structured arguments directly to the tool and uses the same trust review and output contract as a command hook.
L992: ### Configure an MCP tool hook
L993: This hook asks the `scanner` MCP server to scan each patch after Codex writes or edits files:
L994: 
L995:     `{
L996:       "hooks": {
L997:         "PostToolUse": [
L998:           {
L999:             "matcher": "Write|Edit",
L1000:             "hooks": [
L1001:               {
L1002:                 "type": "mcp_tool",
L1003:                 "server": "scanner",
L1004:                 "tool": "scan_patch",
L1005:                 "input": { "patch": "${tool_input.command}" },
L1006:                 "timeout": 30,
L1007:                 "statusMessage": "Scanning edited files"
L1008:               }
L1009:             ]
L1010:           }
L1011:         ]
L1012:       }
L1013:     }`
L1014: Field  | Meaning
L1015: --- | ---
L1016: `type`  | Must be `mcp_tool`.
L1017: `server`  | Required name of an already-connected MCP server.
L1018: `tool`  | Required name of a tool exposed by that server.
L1019: `input`  | Optional JSON object of argument templates. Defaults to `{}`.
L1020: `timeout`  | Optional active execution timeout in seconds. Defaults to `600`.
L1021: `statusMessage`  | Optional message shown while the hook runs.
L1022: ### Expand arguments from the hook event
L1023: 
L1024: Use `${field.nested}` to read a dotted field from the hook event. A placeholder that fills an entire value keeps its JSON type. A placeholder inside a larger string is rendered as text. Codex expands objects and arrays recursively.
L1025: For an event containing `{"tool_input":{"file_path":"src/main.rs","count":3}}`, this argument template:
L1026: 
L1027:     `{
L1028:       "path": "${tool_input.file_path}",
L1029:       "count": "${tool_input.count}",
L1030:       "message": "Scanning ${tool_input.file_path}"
L1031:     }`
L1032: 
L1033: becomes:
L1034: 
L1035:     `{
L1036:       "path": "src/main.rs",
L1037:       "count": 3,
L1038:       "message": "Scanning src/main.rs"
L1039:     }`
L1040: ### Execution and lifecycle
L1041:   * Hooks use an existing MCP connection. They don't start or reconnect servers.
L1042:   * A hook can block an operation when the tool returns a blocking decision. Errors, missing servers, and unavailable tools don't block the operation.
L1043:   * MCP tool hooks run synchronously. They don't request tool approval or trigger other hooks.
L1044:   * The shorter hook or server timeout applies. Time spent waiting for an MCP elicitation response doesn't count against the timeout.
L1045:   * `SessionStart` hooks can run before an MCP server is ready. If that happens, they don't block the session.
L1046:   * `SessionEnd` doesn't support MCP tool hooks.
L1047: ## Turn hooks off
L1048: 
L1049: Hooks are enabled by default. To turn them off in `config.toml`, set:
L1050: 
L1051:     `[features]
L1052:     hooks = false`
L1053: 
L1054: Use `hooks` as the canonical feature key. `codex_hooks` still works as a deprecated alias. Admins can force hooks off the same way in `requirements.toml` with `[features].hooks = false`.
L1055: ## Managed hooks from `requirements.toml`
L1056: Enterprise-managed requirements can also define hooks inline under `[hooks]`. This is useful when admins want to enforce the hook configuration while delivering the actual scripts through MDM or another device-management system. To enforce managed hooks even for users who disabled hooks locally, pin `[features].hooks = true` in `requirements.toml` alongside `[hooks]`. To ignore user, project, session, and plugin hooks while still allowing administrator managed hooks, set `allow_managed_hooks_only = true`.
L1057: 
L1058:     `allow_managed_hooks_only = true
L1059: 
L1060:     [features]
L1061:     hooks = true
L1062: 
L1063:     [hooks]
L1064:     managed_dir = "/enterprise/hooks"
L1065:     windows_managed_dir = 'C:\enterprise\hooks'
L1066: 
L1067:     [[hooks.PreToolUse]]
L1068:     matcher = "^Bash$"
L1069: 
L1070:     [[hooks.PreToolUse.hooks]]
L1071:     type = "command"
L1072:     command = "python3 /enterprise/hooks/pre_tool_use_policy.py"
L1073:     command_windows = 'py -3 C:\enterprise\hooks\pre_tool_use_policy.py'
L1074:     timeout = 30
L1075:     statusMessage = "Checking managed Bash command"`
L1076: Notes for managed hooks:
L1077:   * `managed_dir` is used on macOS and Linux.
L1078:   * `windows_managed_dir` is used on Windows.
L1079:   * Codex doesn't distribute the scripts in `managed_dir`; your enterprise tooling must install and update them separately.
L1080:   * Managed hook commands should use absolute script paths under the configured managed directory.
L1081:   * `allow_managed_hooks_only = true` skips hooks from user, project, session, and plugin sources, but still loads managed hooks from `requirements.toml` and other managed config layers.
L1197: ## Run hooks in the background
L1198: 
L1199: By default, Codex waits for a command hook to finish before continuing the operation that triggered it. Set `async` to `true` to run a command hook in the background while Codex continues.
L1200: ### Configure a background hook
L1201: 
L1202: Add `"async": true` to a command handler in `hooks.json`:
L1203: 
L1204:     `{
L1205:       "hooks": {
L1206:         "PostToolUse": [
L1207:           {
L1208:             "matcher": "Bash",
L1209:             "hooks": [
L1210:               {
L1211:                 "type": "command",
L1212:                 "command": "python3 ~/.codex/hooks/post_tool_use.py",
L1213:                 "async": true,
L1214:                 "timeout": 120
L1215:               }
L1216:             ]
L1217:           }
L1218:         ]
L1219:       }
L1220:     }`
L1221: For an inline hook in `config.toml`, set `async = true`:
L1222: 
L1223:     `[[hooks.PostToolUse]]
L1224:     matcher = "Bash"
L1225: 
L1226:     [[hooks.PostToolUse.hooks]]
L1227:     type = "command"
L1228:     command = "python3 ~/.codex/hooks/post_tool_use.py"
L1229:     async = true
L1230:     timeout = 120`
L1231: Background hooks use the same input, matcher, trust review, timeout, and cite442†large-output handling as synchronous command hooks. As with other command hooks, `timeout` is measured in seconds and defaults to `600`. `Interrupt` hooks use a one-second default and a three-second maximum, including when they run in the background.
L1232: ### How background hooks run
L1233: 
L1234: When a background hook finishes, Codex delivers supported informational output at the next safe point in the conversation:
L1235: 
L1236:   * If a turn is active, Codex waits for the current model request and tool calls to finish, then makes the output available to the next model request in that turn.
L1237:   * If no turn is active, Codex waits until the next user turn. Finishing a background hook doesn't start a new turn.
L1238: Use the same event-specific JSON output as a synchronous hook. Codex adds `additionalContext` to the model's context and surfaces `systemMessage` as a warning.
L1239: 
L1240: Background hooks can't block, approve, rewrite, or otherwise control the operation that triggered them. Use synchronous hooks for tool policies, permission decisions, prompt rejection, or turn continuation.
L1241: ### Limitations
L1242: 
L1243:   * Codex runs up to eight background hooks concurrently per session. Additional hooks wait until a running hook finishes.
L1244:   * Each matching invocation runs independently, and background hooks can finish in a different order than they started.
L1245:   * When the session ends, Codex cancels unfinished background hooks and discards output that hasn't been delivered.
L1246:   * `SessionEnd` hooks always run synchronously.
L1247:

L801: ### Reference
L802: 
L803:   * cite317†CLI customization L804:   * cite318†Developer commands L805:   * cite319†Developer settings L806: # Hooks
L807: 
L808: Run scripts or MCP tools during the Codex lifecycle
L809: 
L810: Copy Page
L811: 
L812: Hooks are an extensibility framework for Codex. They let you run scripts or MCP tools during the agentic loop, enabling features such as:
L813:   * Send the chat to a custom logging/analytics engine
L814:   * Scan your team's prompts to block accidentally pasting API keys
L815:   * Summarize chats to create persistent memories automatically
L816:   * Run a custom validation check when a chat turn stops, enforcing standards
L817:   * Customize prompting when in a certain directory
L818: 
L819: Runtime behavior to keep in mind:
L820:   * Matching hooks from multiple files all run.
L821:   * Multiple matching command hooks for the same event are launched concurrently, so one hook can't prevent another matching hook from starting.
L822:   * Non-managed hooks must be reviewed and trusted before they run.
L823: 
L824: Hooks run at different points in a conversation:
L825: When  | Hooks
L826: --- | ---
L827: During a turn  | `PreToolUse`, `PermissionRequest`, `PostToolUse`, `PreCompact`, `PostCompact`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `SubagentStop`, `Stop`
L828: When you interrupt an active turn  | `Interrupt` (doesn't run for subagents)
L829: When a session or subagent starts  | `SessionStart`, `SubagentStart`
L830: When the main thread ends  | `SessionEnd` (doesn't run for subagents)
L831: ## Where Codex looks for hooks
L832: 
L833: Codex discovers hooks next to active config layers in either of these forms:
L834: 
L835:   * `hooks.json`
L836:   * inline `[hooks]` tables inside `config.toml`
L837: 
L838: Installed plugins can also bundle lifecycle config through their plugin manifest or a default `hooks/hooks.json` file. See cite441†Build plugins†developers.openai.com for the plugin packaging rules.
L839: 
L840: In practice, the four most useful locations are:
L841:   * `~/.codex/hooks.json`
L842:   * `~/.codex/config.toml`
L843:   * `<repo>/.codex/hooks.json`
L844:   * `<repo>/.codex/config.toml`
L845: 
L846: If more than one hook source exists, Codex loads all matching hooks. Higher-precedence config layers don't replace lower-precedence hooks. If a single layer contains both `hooks.json` and inline `[hooks]`, Codex merges them and warns at startup. Prefer one representation per layer.
L847: Codex can also discover hooks bundled with enabled plugins. Plugin-bundled hooks load alongside other hook sources and use the same trust-review flow as other non-managed hooks.
L848: 
L849: Project-local hooks load only when the project `.codex/` layer is trusted. In untrusted projects, Codex still loads user and system hooks from their own active config layers.
L850: ## Review and trust hooks
L851: 
L852: Codex lists configured hooks before deciding which ones can run. Before a non-managed hook can run, Codex requires you to review and trust the exact hook definition. Codex records trust against the hook's current hash, so new or changed hooks are marked for review and skipped until trusted.
L853: Use `/hooks` in the CLI to inspect hook sources, review new or changed hooks, trust hooks, or disable individual non-managed hooks. If hooks need review at startup, Codex prints a warning that tells you to open `/hooks`.
L854: 
L855: Managed hooks from system, MDM, cloud, or `requirements.toml` sources are marked as managed, trusted by policy, and can't be disabled from the user hook browser.
L856: For one-off automation that already vets hook sources outside Codex, pass `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust` to run enabled hooks without requiring persisted hook trust for that invocation.
L857: ## Config shape
L858: 
L859: Hooks are organized in three levels:
L860:   * A hook event such as `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `PreCompact`, `SubagentStart`, or `Stop`
L861:   * A matcher group that decides when that event matches
L862:   * One or more hook handlers that run when the matcher group matches
L863: 
L864:     `{
L865:       "description": "Optional lifecycle hooks for this workspace.",
L866:       "hooks": {
L867:         "SessionStart": [
L868:           {
L869:             "matcher": "startup|resume",
L870:             "hooks": [
L871:               {
L872:                 "type": "command",
L873:                 "command": "python3 ~/.codex/hooks/session_start.py",
L874:                 "statusMessage": "Loading session notes",
L875:                 "additionalContextLimit": 5000
L876:               }
L877:             ]
L878:           }
L879:         ],
L880:         "SessionEnd": [
L881:           {
L882:             "hooks": [
L883:               {
L884:                 "type": "command",
L885:                 "command": "python3 ~/.codex/hooks/session_end.py",
L886:                 "timeout": 3
L887:               }
L888:             ]
L889:           }
L890:         ],
L891:         "PreToolUse": [
L892:           {
L893:             "matcher": "Bash",
L894:             "hooks": [
L895:               {
L896:                 "type": "command",
L897:                 "command": "/usr/bin/python3 \"$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/.codex/hooks/pre_tool_use_policy.py\"",
L898:                 "statusMessage": "Checking Bash command"
L899:               }
L900:             ]
L901:           }
L902:         ],
L903:         "PermissionRequest": [
L904:           {
L905:             "matcher": "Bash",
L906:             "hooks": [
L907:               {
L908:                 "type": "command",
L909:                 "command": "/usr/bin/python3 \"$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/.codex/hooks/permission_request.py\"",
L910:                 "statusMessage": "Checking approval request"
L911:               }
L912:             ]
L913:           }
L914:         ],
L915:         "PostToolUse": [
L916:           {
L917:             "matcher": "Bash",
L918:             "hooks": [
L919:               {
L920:                 "type": "command",
L921:                 "command": "/usr/bin/python3 \"$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/.codex/hooks/post_tool_use_review.py\"",
L922:                 "statusMessage": "Reviewing Bash output"
L923:               }
L924:             ]
L925:           }
L926:         ],
L927:         "UserPromptSubmit": [
L928:           {
L929:             "hooks": [
L930:               {
L931:                 "type": "command",
L932:                 "command": "/usr/bin/python3 \"$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/.codex/hooks/user_prompt_submit_data_flywheel.py\""
L933:               }
L934:             ]
L935:           }
L936:         ],
L937:         "Stop": [
L938:           {
L939:             "hooks": [
L940:               {
L941:                 "type": "command",
L942:                 "command": "/usr/bin/python3 \"$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/.codex/hooks/stop_continue.py\"",
L943:                 "timeout": 30
L944:               }
L945:             ]
L946:           }
L947:         ]
L948:       }
L949:     }`
L950: Notes:
L951:   * `description` is optional top-level metadata for a `hooks.json` file. It doesn't change which hooks run.
L952:   * `timeout` is in seconds.
L953:   * If `timeout` is omitted, Codex uses `600` seconds for most hooks.
L954:     * `SessionEnd` and `Interrupt` use `1` second by default and support up to `3` seconds.
L955:   * `statusMessage` is optional.
L956:   * `additionalContextLimit` sets how much `additionalContext` a command hook can send to the model before Codex saves the full text to disk and sends a shorter preview instead. See cite442†Large hook output .
L957:   * `commandWindows` is an optional Windows-only command override. In TOML, use `command_windows` or `commandWindows`.
L958:   * Set `async` to `true` to cite443†run a command hook in the background .
L959:   * `command` and `mcp_tool` handlers are supported. `prompt` and `agent` handlers are parsed but skipped.
L960:   * Commands run with the session `cwd` as their working directory.
L961:   * For repo-local hooks, prefer resolving from the git root instead of using a relative path such as `.codex/hooks/...`. Codex may be started from a subdirectory, and a git-root-based path keeps the hook location stable.
L962: Equivalent inline TOML in `config.toml`:
L963: 
L964:     `[[hooks.SessionStart]]
L965:     matcher = "^compact$"
L966: 
L967:     [[hooks.SessionStart.hooks]]
L968:     type = "command"
L969:     command = '/usr/bin/python3 "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/.codex/hooks/session_start.py"'
L970:     additionalContextLimit = 5000
L971: 
L972:     [[hooks.PreToolUse]]
L973:     matcher = "^Bash$"
L974: 
L975:     [[hooks.PreToolUse.hooks]]
L976:     type = "command"
L977:     command = '/usr/bin/python3 "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/.codex/hooks/pre_tool_use_policy.py"'
L978:     timeout = 30
